summary.attribution: Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
sentences: The bill would let a child adopted from certain countries under a bilateral deal become an Australian citizen immediately after the adoption is finalised.
It gives adopted children the same entitlement to citizenship as those adopted under the Hague Convention, removing the need for travel documents like a home-country passport or an adoption visa.
The bilateral arrangements covered are those identified in the Family Law (Bilateral Arrangements – Intercountry Adoption) Regulations 1998, currently involving Ethiopia, Korea, and Taiwan.
changes: Creates an entitlement to Australian citizenship for persons adopted under a bilateral arrangement.
Allows the immediate grant of citizenship following the adoption's completion.
Lets the adopted child travel to Australia as an Australian citizen without needing a home country passport or adoption visa.
summary.affected: Australian citizens who adopt a child from Ethiopia, Korea, or Taiwan under a bilateral arrangement.

speeches.speaker: Christopher Pyne
speeches.brief: Updated the House that the Senate had passed the Asset Recycling Fund Bill 2014 with amendments the government would reject and return to the Senate, said debate would move to the Australian Citizenship Amendment (Intercountry Adoption) Bill 2014 in the meantime, and estimated proceedings would finish about half past eight and resume at 11 o'clock the next morning.

speeches.speaker: Mark Dreyfus
speeches.brief: Supported the Australian Citizenship Amendment (Intercountry Adoption) Bill 2014 extending citizenship to children adopted from non-Hague Convention countries including South Korea, Taiwan and Ethiopia, while warning against exploitation risks and recalling that the Ethiopian adoption program was closed in 2012 after being suspended in 2009 and resumed in 2010.

speeches.speaker: Steve Irons
speeches.brief: Supported the intercountry adoption bill while recounting a personal experience as a foster child, noted Australian adoptions fell 77 per cent from 1,501 in 1998-99 to 339 in 2012-13, and urged caution given the royal commission's findings on historical abuse in child migrant institutions, including two in the Swan electorate.

speeches.speaker: Jane Prentice
speeches.brief: Supported the intercountry adoption bill, citing constituent Sean Crookes' account of Ethiopian adoption files stalled for years, noted intercountry adoptions peaked at 434 in 2004-05 before falling to 129 in 2012-13, and welcomed the COAG agreement for a new national intercountry adoption service by early 2015.

speeches.speaker: Ken Wyatt
speeches.brief: Supported the intercountry adoption bill, sharing an anecdote about a man brought from Liverpool as a child migrant who was adopted three or four times but each time returned to the institution, and drew parallels with the film Philomena and Australia's stolen generation in urging safeguards for adopted children's cultural connections.

speeches.speaker: Nickolas Varvaris
speeches.brief: Supported the Australian Citizenship Amendment (Intercountry Adoption) Bill 2014, which grants automatic citizenship to children adopted under bilateral, non-Hague Convention arrangements, citing 129 Australian intercountry adoptions in 2012 to 2013 and average waiting times that had risen from three to five years.

speeches.speaker: Philip Ruddock
speeches.brief: Supported the Australian Citizenship Amendment (Intercountry Adoption) Bill 2014, quoting the Prime Minister's pledge to cut red tape around overseas adoption and his announcement of a new adoption program with South Africa, and praised Deborra-Lee Furness for changing community attitudes toward intercountry adoption.

speeches.speaker: Graham Perrett
speeches.brief: Supported the Australian Citizenship Amendment (Intercountry Adoption) Bill 2014, tracing Australia's history of forced and intercountry adoption including the 2013 national apology for forced adoption, and noted 129 intercountry adoptions were finalised in 2012 to 2013, with Taiwan now the largest source country.

speeches.speaker: Melissa Price
speeches.brief: Argued that the Australian Citizenship Amendment (Intercountry Adoption) Bill 2014 would streamline citizenship for children adopted under bilateral agreements, allowing eligible children to enter Australia without visas and apply for citizenship after overseas finalisation. Supported safeguards aligned with the Hague Convention and cited reduced processing time, cost and stress for adoptive families.

speeches.speaker: Andrew Broad
speeches.brief: Supported the Australian Citizenship Amendment (Intercountry Adoption) Bill 2014, saying it would streamline citizenship for children adopted under bilateral agreements with countries including Taiwan, south Korea and South Africa. Argued that eligible children would no longer need visas and could travel to Australia on Australian passports once adoption was finalised.

speeches.speaker: Eric Hutchinson
speeches.brief: Supported the Australian Citizenship Amendment (Intercountry Adoption) Bill, which grants citizenship to children adopted under bilateral arrangements with countries outside the Hague convention, and noted the Prime Minister's interdepartmental committee, established in December, recommended a new national intercountry adoption service.

speeches.speaker: Fiona Scott
speeches.brief: Supported the Australian Citizenship Amendment (Intercountry Adoption) Bill, saying it would reduce red tape and delays and allow children adopted under bilateral arrangements with non-Hague Convention countries to obtain Australian citizenship and passports before travelling to Australia. Reported that median processing time had risen from 37 months in 2007-08 to 61 months in 2012-13.

speeches.speaker: Don Randall
speeches.brief: Supported the Australian Citizenship Amendment (Intercountry Adoption) Bill 2014, which lets children adopted from bilateral partner countries such as South Korea, Taiwan, South Africa and formerly Ethiopia become Australian citizens automatically rather than needing visas that currently cost $2,370 and can take more than 12 months to process.

speeches.speaker: Ewen Jones
speeches.brief: Supported the Australian Citizenship Amendment (Intercountry Adoption) Bill 2014, which would extend citizenship treatment for children adopted under bilateral arrangements, allowing eligible children to travel to Australia as citizens. Argued that the measure would reduce complexity and cost while retaining safeguards and applying to adoptions finalised before or after commencement.

speeches.speaker: Louise Markus
speeches.brief: Supported the Australian Citizenship Amendment (Intercountry Adoption) Bill, arguing that it would reduce unnecessary red tape and enable children adopted under bilateral arrangements to enter Australia as citizens. Reported that the measure followed reviews and reforms intended to improve intercountry adoption while preserving protections and developing a national system.

speeches.speaker: Bob Baldwin
speeches.brief: Supported the Australian Citizenship Amendment (Intercountry Adoption) Bill 2014 to remove red tape for adopting families, illustrating the case with constituent Dr Samuel Vidler's fight to adopt a foster daughter and another family's struggle to gain residency for a child adopted overseas.

speeches.speaker: Kelly O'Dwyer
speeches.brief: Supported the Australian Citizenship Amendment (Intercountry Adoption) Bill 2014 as a measure to reduce bureaucratic barriers for Australian families adopting from countries with bilateral agreements. Said eligible children would receive Australian citizenship on adoption and travel on Australian passports, while safeguards and the best interests of children remained paramount.

speeches.speaker: Luke Howarth
speeches.brief: Supported the Australian Citizenship Amendment (Intercountry Adoption) Bill 2014, saying it would let children adopted overseas by Australian citizens travel home as citizens without needing a passport or adoption visa, and noted the government had received more than 100 public submissions on overseas adoption reform.

speeches.speaker: Natasha Griggs
speeches.brief: Supported the Australian Citizenship Amendment (Intercountry Adoption) Bill, noting overseas adoptions in Australia fell from a peak of 434 in 2004 to 2005 to just 129 in 2012 to 2013, calling Australia's adoption rate low compared to other developed nations.

speeches.speaker: Teresa Gambaro
speeches.brief: Supported the intercountry adoption bill, detailing that the Interdepartmental Committee on Intercountry Adoption received 108 submissions, of which twenty-six were from organisations and 24 opposed intercountry adoption outright, and that children from South Korea, Taiwan and Ethiopia would now gain citizenship as soon as their adoption is finalised.

speeches.speaker: John Alexander
speeches.brief: Supported the intercountry adoption bill, recounting a constituent, Jo Ellem, who had waited five years for her first adopted child and seven years for a second, and citing the 2005 parliamentary inquiry finding that Australia's per capita overseas adoption rate was less than one-third that of other developed nations.

speeches.speaker: Scott Morrison
speeches.brief: Summed up debate on the Australian Citizenship Amendment (Intercountry Adoption) Bill 2014, explaining that children adopted by Australian citizens under bilateral arrangements would gain the same access to citizenship as those adopted under the Hague Convention, and thanked adoptive parents for their perseverance while commending the bill to the House.
